name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the **real-time, Legal-flagged triage queue** where Legal designates top-priority false positives for immediate review. This cuts response time for high-risk content by 60%—better than waiting for daily batches. The trade-off: Legal must staff this queue 24/7, but the risk of delayed takedowns outweighs the cost.

name: Scriv
text: Legal’s 24/7 queue solves the symptom—delayed takedowns—but not the root: the triage system itself is still reactive. If Legal flags only after the damage spreads, the queue just speeds up the fire drill. Shift the burden upstream: Product must expose the real-time risk signals (e.g., toxicity scores, brand keywords) so Legal can auto-block before the queue even forms. Settle it by running a 48-hour pilot where Product exposes the signals and Legal measures false positives *before* they hit the queue.

name: Chisel
text:
Product must expose real-time risk signals (e.g., toxicity score) directly in the upload interface for Legal to see. This lets Legal triage *before* content spreads, cutting false positives at the source instead of chasing fires. Trade-off: Product must invest in lightweight, visible risk metrics—no extra staffing, but they lose control over how signals are used.

name: Sift
text: The risk metric idea assumes Product can expose toxicity scores without gaming—bad actors will adapt to hit the threshold without changing intent. Better: Legal and Product co-design a *risk-flagging rule* that flags *patterns* (e.g., rapid reposts, cross-platform spread) not just scores—this shifts focus from predicting slurs to stopping their spread. Settle it with a 2-week pilot: Legal tests the rule on 100 uploads, measures false positives vs. spread reduction.

name: Scope
text: Legal and Product jointly build a **real-time "risk pattern" flagger** in the upload interface: it highlights content with *behavioral* red flags (e.g., rapid reposts, cross-platform spread) *before* it spreads. This cuts false positives at the source and eliminates the 24/7 queue burden. Trade-off: Product must expose these patterns in a way that’s hard to game, not just a toxicity score.

name: Scriv
text: The "risk pattern" flagger still assumes Legal and Product can predict every malicious pattern—bad actors will exploit gaps in the rules. Worse, it locks Legal into chasing new patterns instead of fixing the root: Product must expose *real-time intent signals* (e.g., user history, account age) so Legal can act *before* spread. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot: Product builds the intent signals, Legal tests takedown speed vs. false positives—if false positives drop 40% without gaming, adopt it; else, scrap the flagger and staff the 24/7 queue.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Product must expose *real-time intent signals* (e.g., user history, account age, upload frequency) directly in the upload interface for Legal to review *before* content spreads.

**Why:** This stops bad actors at the source by letting Legal block high-risk uploads *before* they go viral, not after. It’s more proactive than chasing patterns or toxicity scores—intent data reveals *who* is trying to game the system, not just *what* they’re posting.

**Trade-off:** Product must invest in real-time user profiling, which raises privacy concerns and requires strict access controls. The alternative—chasing reactive flags—just shifts the burden to Legal without fixing the root cause.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk: exposing intent signals like user history or account age invites gaming—bad actors will spoof clean histories or cycle burner accounts. Better: Legal and Product co-design a *temporal risk score* that decays with account age and penalizes upload bursts, visible in real time. Settle it with a controlled A/B test: compare false positives and takedown lag between the intent-signal prototype and the temporal-score baseline over 30 days.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Product must expose a *temporal risk score* in the upload interface—calculated from account age, upload bursts, and decayed penalties—not raw intent signals. This balances predictability with adaptability, letting Legal block high-risk uploads before they spread while avoiding gaming of static metrics.

**Trade-off:** We accept that bad actors will try to game the score, but the decay and burst penalties make it harder to sustain clean histories long-term, forcing them to either slow down or expose themselves.

name: Sift
text: The temporal risk score still assumes bad actors won’t game the decay window—spoofing account age or cycling burners faster than the penalty decays. Worse, it shifts the burden to Legal to chase dynamic thresholds instead of fixing the root: Product must expose *real-time behavioral signals* (e.g., IP velocity, cross-post timing) that decay *instantly* when gaming is detected. Settle it by running a 30-day pilot where Product exposes both the temporal score *and* raw behavioral signals, measuring which catches more high-risk uploads *before* they spread.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Product must expose *real-time behavioral signals*—upload frequency, cross-posting velocity, and account age—directly in the upload interface for Legal to review *before* content spreads.

**Why:** This stops bad actors at the source by letting Legal block high-risk uploads *before* they go viral, without relying on fragile rules or decaying scores. The trade-off is accepting that some signals can be gamed, but the visibility forces bad actors to work harder to hide, raising their costs enough to deter most abuse.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk: exposing raw behavioral signals like upload frequency or cross-posting velocity invites bad actors to game *those* metrics instead—flooding at lower frequencies or spreading across more accounts. Better: Product and Legal co-design a *latent risk model* that fuses signals into a single, opaque score, updated in real time and only visible to Legal for blocking decisions. Settle it by running a controlled A/B test where one cohort sees raw signals and the other sees the latent score; measure gaming attempts and false positives before scaling.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Product must expose a *latent risk model* in the upload interface—fusing account age, upload bursts, cross-posting velocity, and decay penalties into a single real-time score—visible to Legal before content spreads.

**Why:** This beats gaming by hiding raw signals behind a dynamic model that adapts to spoofing attempts. Legal gets a clear, actionable threshold instead of chasing shifting metrics. The trade-off: we accept a black-box model that’s harder to debug but harder to game.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The latent risk model still leaks *signal fragments*—Legal will infer raw behavioral patterns from score fluctuations, turning the model into a cheat sheet for bad actors. Better: Product and Legal co-design a *black-box risk threshold*—a single binary flag (block/allow) with no score exposed, settled by a signed-off artifact from both teams.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Product must expose a *single binary risk flag* (block/allow) in the upload interface—calculated by a black-box model that fuses account age, upload bursts, cross-posting velocity, and decay penalties—without revealing any raw scores or signal fragments.

**Why:** This eliminates gaming by hiding all behavioral patterns behind a single decision, letting Legal block high-risk uploads before they spread while avoiding signal leakage. The trade-off is reduced transparency for Legal to audit why a decision was made, but predictability and security outweigh debuggability here.

name: Sift
text: Sift: A binary flag still leaks risk logic—Legal will reverse-engineer the model by testing edge cases (e.g., "Why did this 30-day-old account get blocked but this 29-day-old one didn’t?"). Better: expose a *risk tier* (low/medium/high) with a fixed rulebook—e.g., "high = 5+ uploads in 1 hour *and* age < 7 days"—so bad actors can’t game what they can’t see. Settle it by running a 2-week A/B test: measure how often Legal overrides the tier vs. the binary flag.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Product and Legal jointly ship a *risk tier* (low/medium/high) with a fixed, public rulebook—e.g., "high = 5+ uploads in 1 hour *and* cross-posting to 3+ communities"—visible in the upload interface before content spreads.

**Why:** This balances transparency with resistance to gaming. The fixed rules are hard to reverse-engineer, while the tier gives Legal actionable signals without exposing raw metrics. The trade-off: bad actors will still optimize for the rules, but the public rulebook forces them to choose between detectable patterns or stealth—both costly.

name: Scriv
text: The risk tier leaks the rulebook—bad actors will optimize for the edges (e.g., "4 uploads in 59 minutes" or "2 communities"). Instead, Product and Legal should co-design a *latent tier model* that fuses signals into a single score, but only exposes a *range* (e.g., "low: 0-30, medium: 31-70, high: 71-100") with randomized thresholds that shift daily. This forces bad actors to gamble on a moving target, not a fixed rule.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Product and Legal ship a *latent tier model* that fuses signals into a single score, but only exposes a *range* (e.g., "low: 0-30, medium: 31-70, high: 71-100")—with the exact score hidden—visible in the upload interface before content spreads.

**Why:** This blocks gaming by hiding raw signals while giving Legal actionable context. Bad actors can’t reverse-engineer thresholds, and transparency stays high enough to avoid false positives.

**Trade-off:** We accept some loss of debuggability—Legal won’t know *why* a tier was assigned—but that’s the price for making the model opaque to bad actors.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The latent tier still leaks *edges*—bad actors will reverse-engineer the ranges by brute-forcing uploads until the flag flips. Instead, Product and Legal should ship a *randomized tier*—e.g., "low: 0-25, medium: 26-75, high: 76-100" with daily jitter—so the rulebook can’t be gamed. Settle it with a 1-week A/B test: measure upload burst patterns before and after deployment.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Product and Legal ship a *latent tier model* with *daily randomized ranges*—e.g., "low: 0-25, medium: 26-75, high: 76-100" today, but tomorrow it could shift to "low: 0-30, medium: 31-60, high: 61-100"—visible in the upload interface before content spreads.

**Why:** This blocks gaming by making the rulebook unpredictable while keeping the interface transparent. The trade-off is that Legal must accept some opacity in enforcement, but the risk of reverse-engineering drops sharply.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s randomized ranges create a false sense of security—bad actors will still brute-force uploads until they hit the high tier, then back off and repeat. Better: Product and Legal should ship a *latent score* (0-100) with *no tiers exposed*, and only show a warning if the score crosses a hidden threshold—this forces attackers to solve the model, not a moving target. Settle it by running a red-team test: if 100 fake accounts can’t reverse-engineer the threshold in 48 hours, the latent score wins.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Product and Legal ship a *latent score* (0-100) with *no tiers exposed*, and only show a warning if the score crosses a hidden threshold—e.g., "High risk detected. Review pending."

**Why:** This eliminates gaming entirely by removing any actionable thresholds. The trade-off is user confusion—people won’t know *why* they’re flagged—but that’s preferable to bad actors exploiting the system. Legal gets the data they need without tipping off abusers.

name: Scriv
text: Scope’s hidden-score model trades transparency for security—users get no guidance, so they’ll spam appeals or game the warning itself. Instead, Product and Legal should ship a *latent score* with *vague, rotating tiers* (e.g., "low," "elevated," "critical") that change daily, so bad actors can’t map behavior to outcomes. Settle it by A/B testing both: measure brute-force uploads and appeal rates under each model.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Product and Legal ship a *latent score* (0-100) with *no tiers exposed*, but show a *vague, rotating warning* (e.g., "Review pending" or "Escalated")—never the score or tier—visible in the upload interface.

**Why:** This blocks brute-force gaming by hiding all actionable thresholds while giving users *some* feedback to reduce appeals. The trade-off is user confusion—some will spam appeals or ignore warnings—but it’s the only way to fully deny bad actors the ability to reverse-engineer the system.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s "vague, rotating warning" still leaks edges—bad actors will correlate uploads with warning frequency to infer the hidden threshold. Instead, Product and Legal should ship a *latent score* with *no warnings at all* for 90 days, then expose a single static tier (e.g., "low/medium/high") only after the model stabilizes. Settle it by running an A/B test: half the users see no tiers/warnings, half see static tiers—measure appeal rates and gaming attempts.
